accept.reason: Restores headroom after SWE-Bench Verified saturation: the best Pass@1 is 23.3% on the public set and 17.8% on the commercial set, against >70% reported on Verified.
Contamination resistance by licence and access control: a GPL/copyleft public set, a private held-out set and a proprietary commercial set, with different release policies.
accept.location: Section 1 ('exclusively selecting repositories distributed under strong copyleft licenses (GPL)'); Section 3.1; Section 3.3

accept.reason: The commercial set (276 problems, 18 proprietary startup repositories) evaluates agents on code that model developers cannot have trained on, a capability public benchmarks lack.
Tasks are larger than SWE-bench's: reference patches average 107.4 LOC over 4.1 files, at least 10 lines each, more than 100 tasks above 100 lines; Verified has 161 of 500 one-to-two-line problems.
accept.location: Section 1 ('reference solutions span 107.4 lines of code across 4.1 files')

accept.reason: Human augmentation (problem statement, requirements, interface) targets false negatives from underspecification and misnamed interfaces, with a full worked instance.
Test hygiene: tests are run three times and inconsistent ones dropped; annotators drop fail2pass tests that are too broad or irrelevant; Docker environments are built by engineers and auto-verified.
accept.location: Section 3.2 (Tests: 'we run each set of tests 3 times'); Section 4.3

accept.reason: The public set (731 instances) is released on HuggingFace, pre-built Docker images are promised, data and code links are given (removed for review), and the full judge prompt is in the appendix.
accept.location: Section 3.2 (Environments); Section 3.3; title page links; Appendix B.1

accept.reason: Diversity: 41 actively maintained repositories across consumer apps, B2B services and developer tools; Python, Go, JS and TS; feature requests and bug fixes; a per-repository cap.
Per-language and per-repository breakdowns show heterogeneity (Go and Python higher; some repositories below 10% for all models).
A trajectory-level failure taxonomy across six models, with the full judge prompt, distinguishes e.g. Sonnet 4's context overflow from Opus 4.1's wrong solutions.
Controlled comparison: one scaffold (SWE-Agent), the same prompt for all models, a 200-turn cap, stated hosting (vLLM, 8xH100) and model date.
The task format is easy to understand from a full worked instance (problem statement, requirements, interface) and an original-vs-rewritten comparison.
Candid limitations: language coverage, dependence on test suites, and that augmentation 'may inadvertently make problems too prescriptive'.
A held-out set of 858 problems from 12 repositories is reserved for future overfitting checks against the public set.

reject.reason: Text and Table 1 disagree: the text gives Claude Sonnet 4 16.3% and GPT-4o 3.9%, Table 1 gives 17.6% and 4.9%; the text also calls Qwen-3 32B 'DeepSeek Qwen-3 32B'.
reject.location: Section 5 Results ('also achieves a 16.3% resolve rate') vs Table 1 (17.6, 4.9); cross-referenced
reject.fix: Align the text with Table 1; fix the model name. Minutes.

reject.reason: Table 3's failure counts cannot come from the stated population. Section 6.2 filters 'to only unresolved instances' of the public set (N=731), yet Submitted+Not-submitted is 920 for Opus 4.1 (expected about 565 unresolved), 915 for Gemini (about 632), 792 for Qwen (about 706), 789 for GPT-4o (about 695), 724 for GPT-5 (about 561) and 699 for Sonnet 4 (about 602). Four totals exceed 731. The unit of analysis is unknown, so every percentage in Table 3 and Section 6.2 is uninterpretable.
reject.location: Table 3 vs Table 1 and Section 6.2 ('programmatically filter to only unresolved instances'); recomputed by P1
reject.fix: State the unit (runs? attempts? sets?), recompute Table 3 on the unresolved public instances, and correct the text. Hours, given the trajectories.

reject.reason: Section 6.2 and Section 1 make failure-mode claims that Table 3 contradicts. Qwen 3 32B 'exhibits the highest tool error rate (42.0%)', but Table 3 gives Qwen 349/792 = 44.1% of failures, and GPT-5 has 446/724 = 61.6%. Section 1 says smaller models 'more frequently fail due to issues in syntax', but syntax errors are 223/920 = 24.2% of Opus 4.1's failures against 184/792 = 23.2% of Qwen's.
reject.location: Section 6.2 ('exhibits the highest tool error rate (42.0%)'); Section 1; Table 3; recomputed by P2
reject.fix: Rewrite the failure-mode conclusions from corrected counts (after R2). Hours.

reject.reason: The central claim of contamination resistance is never tested. The held-out set is not evaluated, there is no public-vs-held-out comparison, no commit-date-vs-cutoff analysis and no memorization probe. The GPL argument ('legal barriers') is asserted, not shown, and the public set's commits and gold patches are already in public git history.
reject.location: Section 3.1 ('we ensure benchmark content is unlikely to appear in proprietary model training sets'); Section 5 ('we keep the private set held-out for future analysis'); checked by P3
reject.fix: Evaluate the held-out set with the same models and report the public-vs-held-out gap; stratify public results by commit date relative to model cutoffs; soften the legal claim. Days of compute.

reject.reason: The 'long-horizon' framing and the 'hours to days for a professional software engineer' estimate are not backed by any measurement. Difficulty is operationalized only by LOC and file counts, and the requirements and interface name exact files, functions and URLs, which removes much of the exploration that makes real tasks long. Basis: contribution check, question 2.
reject.location: Title; Abstract ('may require hours to days for a professional software engineer'); Section 1 (LOC/files); Section 5 Issue Ambiguity ('after being given significant details'); Appendix A.2-A.3; checked by P4
reject.fix: Report human solve-time estimates on a sample, or agent steps and turns per task; otherwise narrow the title and abstract. A small annotation study, or a wording change.

reject.reason: The public-commercial gap is attributed to 'the greater complexity of enterprise codebases' without controls. The commercial set's size, language and LOC statistics are not reported, it averages 15 problems per repository against 66 for the public set, and model rankings change (Sonnet 4 is third on the public set at 17.6%, fourth on the commercial set at 9.1%).
reject.location: Section 1 ('underscoring the greater complexity of enterprise codebases'); Section 5; Table 1 vs Table 2; Figure 3 caption ('Distributions in the public set'); checked by P5
reject.fix: Report commercial-set statistics and compare resolve rates stratified by LOC, files and language, or present the gap as descriptive. Hours.

reject.reason: Single run, Pass@1, no uncertainty. With N=731, the 95% binomial interval is about +/-3.1 pp at 23%, so GPT-5 (23.3) and Opus 4.1 (22.7) are not separable; the commercial set (N=276) gives about +/-4.5 pp. 'GPT-5 achieving the highest score' is not supported as a ranking.
reject.location: Abstract; Table 1; Table 2; derived in P11
reject.fix: Report binomial or bootstrap CIs; run 3 seeds for the top models on the public set. Cheap for CIs; about 3x compute for seeds.

reject.reason: One scaffold only, so the model comparisons are confounded with scaffold fit. Agentless is dismissed without numbers. GPT-5 ends without submitting in 63.1% of its failures, 97.6% of them tool-use failures, which points to a tool-format mismatch. Open-weight models get tool use through 'syntax parsing'.
reject.location: Section 5 Scaffold ('Agentless has difficulty in multi-file editing, thus, produces low evaluation scores'); Section 5 Evaluation settings; Table 3 (GPT-5 Not-Submitted 63.1%, Tool-Use 97.6%); checked by P6
reject.fix: Report the Agentless numbers and run a second scaffold (e.g. OpenHands or a vendor-native agent) on the public set for the top models. Days of compute.

reject.reason: The '>70% on SWE-Bench Verified' contrast that motivates the benchmark comes from external reports under different scaffolds, not from a run under this paper's SWE-Agent, 200-turn, same-prompt setting. The size of the drop is therefore not measured.
reject.location: Section 1 ('over 70% pass rate on SWE-Bench-Verified [15]'); Figure 2 caption; Section 8; checked by P7
reject.fix: Run the same models under the same scaffold on SWE-Bench Verified and report both numbers side by side. A day of compute.

reject.reason: The human augmentation and verification pipeline (C3) is described but not quantified: no number or expertise of annotators, no time per task, no agreement or QA audit, no attrition per stage. The claim that requirements 'don't leak solutions' is asserted, not audited, although the example requirements name exact file paths and function names.
reject.location: Section 3.2; Section 4.2; Section 4.3; Appendix A.2 ('Requirements never include specific code implementation and don't leak solutions'); checked by P8
reject.fix: Report pipeline statistics (annotators, hours, drops per stage, tests removed) and an independent leakage audit on a random sample. Low cost if logs exist.

reject.reason: No ablation of the augmentation components, so neither the false-negative claim nor the source of difficulty is tested. The paper itself says 'the setting without requirements is potentially interesting'.
reject.location: Section 3.1; Section 5 Issue Ambiguity; Section 7.1; checked by P8
reject.fix: Evaluate 2-3 models on the public set with problem statement only, +requirements and +interface. Two extra runs per model.

reject.reason: The construction pipeline refines SWE-bench's: commit-pair sourcing, fail2pass/pass2pass tests, Docker environments and human verification 'Similar to SWE-Bench Verified'. The deltas are licence-based repository selection, private and commercial sets, requirements/interface augmentation and a size filter. That is moderate novelty (contribution check, question 3). The claim to be 'the first to systematically apply such a methodology' is not checked against prior private or held-out benchmarks [verify]. Prior work: SWE-bench [13], SWE-bench Verified [15], LiveBench [19], SWE-bench-Live [25].
reject.location: Section 1 ('the first to systematically apply such a methodology'); Section 3.1 ('Similar to SWE-Bench Verified'); Section 4.1; checked by P10
reject.fix: Position the deltas explicitly against SWE-bench, Verified and time-based contamination-free benchmarks, and qualify the 'first' claim. Writing only.

reject.reason: No quantitative comparison with prior SWE benchmarks (patch size, files, languages, repositories, contamination strategy). Related benchmarks that test the same capabilities are missing, including SWE-Lancer (freelance tasks with end-to-end tests), SWE-Gym, LiveCodeBench (time-based contamination control) and SWE-smith, which is evaluated as a model but not cited.
reject.location: Section 2.1; Section 5 ('fine-tuned on SWE-bench-like trajectories (e.g. SWE-Smith)')
reject.fix: Add a comparison table and the missing related work. Writing only.

reject.reason: The LLM-judge failure analysis is not validated for this setup. The 87% alignment is borrowed from [22], a different judge and taxonomy; the 20-turn choice is said to have 'the highest correspondence with human validations' with no numbers; GPT-5 judges its own trajectories; and Table 3's buckets do not match the categories in Appendix B.1 (no mapping is given).
reject.location: Section 6.2 ('Our work follows Yang et al. [22], who demonstrate 87% alignment'); Table 3; Appendix B.1
reject.fix: Human-label about 100 trajectories and report agreement per bucket; add a judge that is not one of the evaluated models; give the bucket mapping. A day of annotation.

reject.reason: Statistics are reported for the public set only (Figure 3). Patch size, file count, language mix and per-repository counts of the commercial and held-out sets are not given.
reject.location: Figure 3 caption ('Distributions in the public set'); Section 3.3
reject.fix: Add a statistics table for all three sets. Cheap.

reject.reason: The per-repository instance count is inconsistent: Section 1 says each repository contributes 'between 50 and 100 instances, with a strict cap of 100', Section 3.1 says '50-100+ instances', and the commercial set has 276/18 = 15.3 per repository.
reject.location: Section 1; Section 3.1; Section 3.3 (276 problems, 18 repositories; derived)
reject.fix: Correct the statement and give per-repository counts per set. Minutes.

reject.reason: Figure 1's caption names 'difficulty filtering', but the only filter described is the size and multi-file rule. If any model-based filtering was used, the low headline scores are partly by construction.
reject.location: Figure 1 caption ('difficulty filtering'); Section 1; Section 3.1; probed by P9

reject.reason: Decoding settings (temperature, sampling), context-window handling, cost and token budgets, exact model identifiers and the agent prompt are not given; the prompt is only 'a basic prompt outlining the task'.
reject.location: Section 5 Evaluation settings

reject.reason: The commercial and held-out sets are private, and no governance is described: who runs evaluations, how often, how submissions work, and when held-out results are released. The commercial results cannot be reproduced by others; the paper only says it 'will update in the leaderboard'.
reject.location: Section 3.3 ('will update in the leaderboard'); Section 5 Evaluation sets
reject.fix: Describe the evaluation service, release policy and versioning; publish environment hashes and per-instance commercial results by ID. Writing and policy.
